newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Relatives of Irish bomb victims seek police files.
newsitem.headline: Relatives of Irish bomb victims seek police files.

text.p: Relatives of Irish bomb victims killed in the worst day's carnage in the 28-year "Troubles" went to the Dublin High Court on Monday to get police to throw open their files on the case.

Scenting a high-level cover-up, solicitors acting for families of the 33 people killed in two 1974 bomb attacks want the Irish police to allow them to see files on a case in which no one has ever been charged.
"I'm 73 and I won't die happy until I see the bastard that put the bomb under that car and blew my son (Dessie) to bits," Annie Massey told Irish television.
It was the second time in a month that families of people bereaved in the Northern Ireland conflict had sought fresh investigation into some of the 3,200 deaths of the conflict.

Last month relatives of 14 people killed when British paratroopers fired on a 1972 civil rights demonstration in the Northern Ireland city of Londonderry presented the Irish government with new evidence into the "Bloody Sunday" slayings.
The families want an apology for what they say were unprovoked killings by soldiers armed with sophisticated weapons firing into an unarmed crowd.
An official 1972 investigation said the soldiers believed they were under fire from Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas and exonerated them from any wrong-doing.
Northern Ireland's pro-British Loyalist guerrillas are thought to have carried out the twin 1974 bomb attacks in Dublin and Monaghan in reprisal for attacks by IRA gunmen fighting rule from London.
But Irish republicans believe that British security forces may have been involved to intimidate their supporters in the Irish republic, a charge the London government says is ludicrous.
Solicitors want the Irish police to make available all documents relating to the case including communications with the Northern Ireland police force, the Royal Ulster Constabulary.
They suspect that Northern Ireland's police, under pressure from the British government, did not rigorously pursue the case and want to see documentation about the investigation.
The Dublin and Monaghan bombs killed 22 and five people respectively but the death toll rose to 33 after six people injured by the explosions died of their wounds.
It was the biggest day's death toll in the Northern Ireland conflict and marked a turning point in hostilities between pro- Irish and pro-British activists.
The bombs exploded without warning in busy Dublin streets and in the border town of Monaghan after months of IRA attacks on police and British troops in Northern Ireland.
The Ulster Volunteer Force, an outlawed Loyalist guerrilla organisation, has twice tried to bomb targets in Dublin in the past three years in reprisal for IRA attacks but the attempts were bungled.
The Irish government, Britain's partner in the search for a lasting Northern Ireland settlement, says it is collating new evidence into the Bloody Sunday killings and will hand it over to Britain.

The evidence, in a book and legal studies, purports to show that a sniper or snipers fired on the crowd from a high vantage point, contradicting the soldiers' testimony that the only shooting which took place was at ground level.
